Empirical Research Plan  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Cross-sectional two-stage least squares (2SLS) / IV.  

• Why IV?  
  – We need the causal effect of current institutional quality (endogenous—shaped by history, reverse causality, and omitted geography) on current income.  
  – The data offer a plausibly exogenous historical shock—European settler mortality (17th–19th C.)—that affected colonisers’ ability to settle and hence the type of institutions transplanted.  
  – Mortality is determined by the pre-germ-theory disease environment; conditional on broad geography it should influence 20th-century income only through institutions.  
Hence a cross-sectional IV is the cleanest design; DID/event-study/RDD are not feasible because treatment timing is centuries ago and no sharp threshold exists.

Equation system  
First stage:  
  Insti_i = α + π ln(SettlerMortality_i) + X_i'γ + ε_i¹  

Second stage:  
  lnGDP_i = β Ĩnsti_i + X_i'δ + ε_i²  

X_i = latitude, continent dummies, legal origin, religion, natural-resource and health controls, etc.


--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment (“dose” variable):  
  Insti_i = 1985–95 average protection-from-expropriation index (0–10, higher = better).

Counterfactual (“control”):  
  Countries with lower protection scores—they form part of the same cross-section; identification relies on exogenous variation in settlers’ mortality, not on an explicit untreated group.

Instrument (Z):  
  ln(SettlerMortality_i) = log of annualised deaths per 1,000 mean strength for European soldiers, sailors, and bishops stationed 1600–1875.

Timing:  
  Z is measured 17th–19th C.; Insti_i in late 20th C.; outcome in 1988–95. No separate running variable or cutoff (not an RDD).


--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance: Higher settler mortality made it hard to establish large European settlements ⇒ lower-quality institutions.  
      Plausibility: Documented historical narrative; easily testable in first stage (expect π < 0, F-stat > 10).

A2. Exclusion restriction: Conditional on controls, settler mortality affects present-day income only through its effect on institutions (no direct channel).  
      Plausibility: Diseases lethal to Europeans had small long-run effect on indigenous adults; modern medicine eliminated them. We still include latitude, climate, malaria ecology, soil, and natural resources to help satisfy this.

A3. Independence / Ignorability: Mortality rates are as-good-as-random with respect to un-observables that drive modern income, conditional on controls.  
      Plausibility: Mortality was driven by disease ecology exogenous to 17th-century European choice of colonies; documented before colonisation patterns were set.

A4. SUTVA: Institutional quality of country i does not affect income in country j once we treat countries as units.  
      Plausibility: Some spillovers exist (trade, war) but unlikely to be systematically correlated with the instrument.

A5. Monotonicity (LATE): Countries with high settler mortality were never more likely to adopt inclusive institutions (no “defiers”).  
      Plausibility: Historically, higher mortality either deterred settlement or induced extractive structures.


--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Omitted geographic/productivity factors correlated with mortality (e.g., tropical cash crops, soil).  
    • Mitigation: Control for 15+ geo-climatic covariates (latitude, ruggedness, precipitation, soil suitability, natural-resource wealth) and show results are stable.

T2. Direct disease legacy: Historical malaria regions may remain unhealthy, lowering income directly.  
    • Mitigation: Include 1960 malaria ecology index, life expectancy, infant mortality in 1960; show coefficient on mortality disappears when institutions are controlled but malaria variable remains.

T3. Measurement error in mortality data (heterogeneous record quality).  
    • Mitigation: (i) Use log form to reduce influence of outliers; (ii) show robustness to dropping observations with imputed mortality; (iii) jackknife (leave-one-out) first stage.


--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)    # fast data handling
library(fixest)        # OLS and IV with clustered SEs
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and merge data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Assume three csv files: income.csv, institutions.csv, history.csv
dt_income  <- fread("income_1995.csv")        # country, ln_gdp95
dt_inst    <- fread("institutions_8595.csv")  # country, exprop85_95
dt_hist    <- fread("settler_mortality.csv")  # country, settler_mort

controls   <- fread("controls.csv")           # latitude etc.

dt <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y,by="country",all=FALSE),
             list(dt_income, dt_inst, dt_hist, controls))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
dt[, ln_gdp := log(gdp_ppp_1995)]
dt[, ln_s_mort := log(settler_mort)]                  # instrument
dt[, inst := exprop85_95 ]                            # treatment

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Baseline 2SLS
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
iv_formula <- ln_gdp ~ inst + lat + africa + legal_origin + malaria60 +
                         soil_quality + natural_resources |
                         ln_s_mort + lat + africa + legal_origin +
                         malaria60 + soil_quality + natural_resources

mod_iv <- feols(iv_formula, data = dt, se = "hetero")   # HC1 SEs
summary(mod_iv)

# First-stage diagnostics
mod_fs <- feols(inst ~ ln_s_mort + lat + africa + legal_origin +
                          malaria60 + soil_quality + natural_resources,
                data = dt, se = "hetero")
summary(mod_fs)                  # Check F-stat > 10

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: add alternative institution measure
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
iv_formula_dem <- ln_gdp ~ democracy_1900 + lat + africa |
                            ln_s_mort + lat + africa
mod_iv_dem <- feols(iv_formula_dem, data = dt, se = "hetero")
summary(mod_iv_dem)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Sensitivity: Jackknife (leave-one-out)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
jack_est <- lapply(unique(dt$country), function(ctry){
   feols(iv_formula, data = dt[country != ctry], se = "hetero")$coeftable["inst","Estimate"]
})
print(summary(unlist(jack_est)))
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Sign (+): Better protection from expropriation → higher income.  
Magnitude (prior): A 1-point rise (≈1 SD) in the 0–10 index should raise log GDP per capita by roughly 0.5–0.7 log points (≈65–100 %). Equivalently, moving from the 25th to 75th percentile of institutional quality would plausibly double income.

Geography conditional on institutions: coefficients on latitude or “Africa” dummies should fall sharply and may become statistically insignificant once institutions are instrumented.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)  

C1. Relevance (first-stage F > 10) .......... 1  
C2. Exclusion restriction credible .......... 0.5  
C3. No remaining geographic confounds ........ 0.5  
C4. No measurement error in Z ................ 0.5  
C5. SUTVA / no cross-country spillovers ...... 0.5  

Total ≈ 3/5. Instrument is strong and historically grounded; remaining concerns revolve around exclusion and data quality, to be probed in robustness checks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan leverages a historically exogenous source of variation to isolate the long-run causal effect of property-rights institutions on economic performance while transparently addressing the main threats to validity.
